era: The Third Caliph — Keeper of the Mus'haf
teaser: He was reciting the Qur'an when they came for him. The blood on the page stopped at one ayah.
quran_mention: The Pledge of Ridwan was taken on his behalf while he was absent: «لَقَدْ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ إِذْ يُبَايِعُونَكَ تَحْتَ الشَّجَرَةِ» — 'Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged to you under the tree.' (48:18)

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: A rich man who drew his own water at night
layers.content:
Uthman ibn Affan ibn Abi al-As ibn Umayya ibn Abd Shams ibn Abd Manaf ibn Qusayy. His mother was Arwa bint Kurayz, and her mother was al-Bayda bint Abd al-Muttalib — so he was a grandson of the Prophet's own great-grandfather's line. Before Islam his kunya was Abu Amr. He took a new one, Abu Abdullah, from the son Ruqayya bore him.

He was a merchant in the Jahiliyya and stayed a merchant in Islam, lending money in profit-sharing partnerships. Those who knew him described a man neither short nor tall, handsome, soft-skinned, wide-shouldered and large-jointed, with a great heavy beard he dyed yellow. He wore a Yamani cloak worth eight hundred dirhams. He also had gold braces on his teeth.

And he carried his own water. Told he could order a servant to fill the wudu jug at night, he refused: 'No, the night is a time in which they rest.' al-Hasan once found him asleep in the mosque with his cloak folded under his head. When a child was born to him he would pray over the infant still in its swaddling and lean in to smell it, explaining simply that he wanted the child to have something of his heart.
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Uthman is the truest of my community in modesty' — narrated by Anas ibn Malik, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: A voice on the Syria road, then a rope
layers.content:
He came in early, with Talha ibn Ubaydullah, following az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam. The Prophet ﷺ set Islam before them, recited to them, told them what it required and what Allah promised. They believed on the spot.

Then Uthman offered something. 'Messenger of Allah, I have just come from Syria. When we were between Ma'an and az-Zarqa, we were sleeping when a caller called to us: Sleepers, arise. Ahmad has emerged in Makka. We came and heard of you.' He entered Islam before the Prophet ﷺ had even begun teaching in the house of al-Arqam.

The cost came from inside the family. His uncle al-Hakam ibn Abi al-As took him and bound him with rope. 'Will you leave the religion of your father for a new religion? By Allah, I will never let you go until you leave this religion.' Uthman answered without moving: 'By Allah, I will never leave it or abandon it.' His uncle held him, saw that nothing was going to bend, and let him go.

He then emigrated twice to Abyssinia, both times with his wife Ruqayya, the Prophet's daughter. Of that departure the Prophet ﷺ said: 'He was the first to emigrate to Allah after Lut.'
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ said of Uthman's emigration: 'He was the first to emigrate to Allah after Lut' — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley (narration of Yazid ibn Ruman)

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: The hand the Prophet ﷺ pledged on his behalf
layers.content:
He missed Badr. The Prophet ﷺ left him in Madinah in charge of Ruqayya, who was dying, and she died the day Zayd ibn Harithah rode in with news of the victory. The Prophet ﷺ gave him a share of the spoils and the reward, so that he counted as one who had been there. Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ married him to a second daughter, Umm Kulthum, and said: 'If I had a third daughter, I would marry her to Uthman.'

At al-Hudaybiyah he was chosen as envoy because his clan in Makkah could shield him. Quraysh offered him a private umrah since he had come this far. He refused it: how could he take that while the Prophet ﷺ was being kept out. Then he was late returning, and a rumour spread that Quraysh had killed him. The Muslims began pledging under the tree not to flee. The Prophet ﷺ held out his own hand and said, 'This is for Uthman,' and took the pledge on his behalf. That is the Pledge of Ridwan.

Before Tabuk he equipped the army out of his own caravan — camels, gold, a thousand dinars — until his giving reached nine hundred camels and a hundred horses.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 48:18 — 'Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged to you under the tree'
layers.hadith_ref: At al-Hudaybiyah the Prophet ﷺ held out his own hand and said 'This is for Uthman' — al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: Besieged, and refusing to let Muslims fight Muslims
layers.content:
The council of six that Umar left behind settled on him. Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf gave allegiance first, then Ali. Ibn Mas'ud used to say from the minbar in Kufa: 'We put in command the best of those who remain, and we were not negligent.' Uthman's first words to the people were not a programme but an apology: 'The beginning of the ride is difficult. There will be days after today. If I live, I will address you properly. We are not orators. Allah will teach us.'

Years later his house in Madinah was under siege. He sent for al-Ashtar and asked him plainly what the people wanted. Three things, he was told: hand the matter back to them, or submit to retaliation, or be fought. He refused the first — he would not take off a garment Allah had placed on him. Then he said what is more remembered than any of it: 'By Allah, I prefer to come out and have my head struck off than to let loose the community of Muhammad against one another.'

He warned them where this road went. Kill me, he said, and you will never love one another afterwards, nor pray together, nor face an enemy together again. Muslims to this day differ in how they judge those months. What is not in dispute is that he would not buy his own safety with their blood.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley (narration of Waththab, freedman of Umar)

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: One Qur'an, one reading, one page stained
layers.content:
On the morning of the day he died he told his companions a dream: 'I saw the Messenger of Allah last night and he told me, Uthman, you will break the fast with us.' He fasted that day.

They came over the wall of the neighbouring house. They found him with his wife Na'ila and an open copy of the Qur'an, reciting Surah al-Baqarah. When the first blow landed he said, 'In the Name of Allah. I have put my trust in Allah.' The blood ran down his beard onto the page. The narration of his family says it came to rest at «فَسَيَكْفِيكَهُمُ اللَّهُ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ» — 'Allah will be enough for you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.' He covered the mus'haf. Na'ila stood over the looting afterwards and said: by Allah, you killed him while he was fasting, standing in prayer, reciting the Qur'an.

What the ummah kept from him is in every hand that opens a Qur'an. He sent for the pages Hafsah held, set Zayd ibn Thabit and three Qurayshi companions to copy them, ruled that where they differed on a word they write it in the tongue of Quraysh, and dispatched the copies out to the provinces. That is the text you read tonight.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 2:137 — 'Allah will be enough for you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing'
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an — narrated by Anas ibn Malik, on Uthman's copying of the mus'haf
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley; Sahih al-Bukhari

quiz.prompt: Who bound Uthman with rope to make him renounce Islam?

options.text: Abu Jahl
His uncle al-Hakam ibn Abi al-As
Umayya ibn Khalaf
His own father Affan

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III — reported from Ibrahim ibn al-Harith at-Taymi
quiz.scholar_reflection: The uncle held him until he was satisfied nothing would bend, then released him. Uthman's answer never changed: 'By Allah, I will never leave it or abandon it.'

quiz.prompt: Why was Uthman absent from the Battle of Badr?

options.text: He was still in Abyssinia
He was trading in Syria
The Prophet ﷺ left him with his daughter Ruqayya, who was gravely ill
He was governing Madinah while the army was away

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III — narrated by Abdullah ibn Miknaf al-Ansari
quiz.scholar_reflection: She died the day the news of victory reached Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ gave him a share and the reward of Badr anyway, so he stood among those counted present.

quiz.prompt: Quraysh offered Uthman a private umrah while he was their envoy at al-Hudaybiyah. What did he do?

options.text: Accepted, and performed it quickly before returning
Refused, because the Prophet ﷺ was being denied it
Asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission first
Accepted on condition all the Muslims could enter

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the mission of Uthman to Quraysh
quiz.scholar_reflection: His delay in returning bred the rumour that he had been killed, and the Muslims began pledging under the tree. The Prophet ﷺ put out his own hand and said, 'This is for Uthman.'

quiz.prompt: What did Uthman say when he was told he could hand the caliphate back and end the siege, or else be fought?

options.text: 'Bring me my sword and let Allah judge between us'
'I will step down if the Muhajirun agree'
'I prefer to have my head struck off than to let loose the community of Muhammad against one another'
'Send for Mu'awiya and let him decide'

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III — narrated by Waththab, the freedman of Umar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He also refused to take off a garment he believed Allah had placed on him. Muslims differ in how they weigh those months; his refusal to spill Muslim blood for his own safety is not among the disputed parts.

quiz.prompt: What is Uthman most remembered for leaving the ummah as caliph?

options.text: The first written collection of hadith
A single agreed written Qur'an, copied and sent to the provinces
The Islamic calendar
The system of provincial judges

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an — narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: He gathered the pages Hafsah kept, appointed Zayd ibn Thabit with three Qurayshi companions to copy them, and settled disputed words in the dialect of Quraysh. Every mus'haf since traces to that decision.

quiz.prompt: Uthman would not let a servant fetch his water at night because 'the night is a time in which they rest.' Where do you notice the people who serve you?

options.text: I try to, but mostly when it costs me nothing
I think about it and still choose my own convenience
I would rather do a thing myself than ask
Honestly, I rarely think about it at all

quiz.citation: Reflection on the account of Abdullah ar-Rumi, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was one of the wealthiest men in Madinah and the head of state. The measure of a man is often in what he will not ask someone else to do.

quiz.prompt: He refused an umrah he badly wanted because the Prophet ﷺ could not have it. When have you turned down something permitted out of loyalty?

options.text: I take what is offered — it helps no one to refuse
I have declined things so as not to be set apart
It depends how much I want the thing
I have never been offered an advantage worth refusing

quiz.citation: Reflection on Uthman at al-Hudaybiyah, al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was standing at the edge of the Haram with permission in hand. Refusing it gained him nothing anyone could see, and the Prophet ﷺ pledged with his own hand for him.

quiz.prompt: His giving for Tabuk kept escalating — camels, then gold, then more camels — long past the point of enough. What stops your generosity?

options.text: A number I have quietly decided on in advance
The point where it starts to affect my own plans
Nothing, if I believed the cause completely
I give steadily and small rather than in bursts

quiz.citation: Reflection on the equipping of the army of Tabuk, al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: The army for Tabuk was assembled in hardship and heat, and his caravan had been loaded for trade. He unloaded it. There is no ceiling recorded in the account.

quiz.prompt: Besieged, he was told exactly what would follow if he fought back — and chose not to. How do you weigh peace against being in the right?

options.text: Being right matters; someone has to hold the line
I would rather lose the argument than break the relationship
I tell myself I choose peace and then keep score
It depends entirely on who else gets hurt

quiz.citation: Reflection on the siege of Uthman's house, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He predicted what the killing would cost: that they would never love one another, pray together, or face an enemy together again. He chose to be the one who absorbed it.

quiz.prompt: He spent his last morning fasting on the strength of a dream, and his last minutes reciting. What would your last hour default to?
quiz.slider_label: What you return to at the end

options.text: Whatever I already do daily — nothing new appears
Prayer, though I do not pray like that now
The people I love, before anything else
I would not know until it arrived

quiz.citation: Narrated by Nafi and by the family of Uthman — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Nothing about that morning was staged. He was doing what he did every day, and the day happened to be his last.
